This research introduces FPIO, a novel few-shot parsing model that achieves state-of-the-art results on semantic parsing with limited annotated data. FPIO's architecture is based on a graph neural network that incorporates a node attention mechanism, allowing it to effectively process complex tree structures. By utilizing a shared node representation, FPIO can efficiently handle tasks with varying input sizes. Through an extensive evaluation on 12 datasets, FPIO demonstrates superior performance to existing few-shot parsing methods, even when trained with as few as 10 annotated examples.

This study investigates the impact of diverse training data on the resilience of speech recognition models to speaker and topic variations. We found that a model's ability to generalize improves with increased diversity, but only up to a certain point. After that, further data, although diverse, fails to enhance the model's performance. We also discovered that a model's performance on out-of-domain data is better predicted by its performance on a range of related topics rather than its performance on in-domain data.

A study of 15 Be-type binary systems has been conducted, using data from the MIRC-X instrument at the CHARA array, to determine the binary orbital parameters. The results show that the binary systems have eccentric orbits, with eccentricities ranging from 0.2 to 0.9. The orbital periods of the binary systems are relatively short, with most being less than 10 days. The study found that the binary systems have a higher frequency of orbital periods than normal B-type binary systems, with a peak frequency of 0.15 per day. The study also found that the binary systems have a higher frequency of orbital periods than Be-type binary systems, with a peak frequency of 0.05 per day. The study suggests that the binary systems have a higher frequency of orbital periods due to the effects of tidal forces.

This study presents a novel data augmentation approach for improving the performance of ITN models when trained on in-domain data. The method involves generating a dataset of out-of-domain text using a pre-trained language model, which is then combined with in-domain data to enhance the model's generalizability. Experimental results on two datasets demonstrate that this technique surpasses traditional in-domain training methods and achieves comparable performance to models trained on larger, out-of-domain datasets.

The Faber-Krahn inequality for the Hermite operator is established, providing a lower bound for its first eigenvalue in terms of its isoperimetric quotient. This inequality is then refined to account for the optimal shape, revealing that the optimal configuration is a torus-shaped droplet.

Recent studies have demonstrated that neural tangent kernels (NTKs) can effectively approximate the behavior of deep neural networks (DNNs) when trained with gradient descent. This approximation enables the use of closed-form solutions for NTKs, which can be more interpretable and computationally efficient than their neural network counterparts. This paper presents a novel approach to integrating NTKs with a graph convolutional framework, which can be applied to semi-supervised classification tasks on graph-structured data. This method is evaluated on a range of real-world datasets and is found to achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art graph convolutional models while offering improved interpretability and computational efficiency.

In a non-Hermitian chain like the Hatano-Nelson model, where site occupation is reduced at the edges, the standard skin effect is altered. The influence of correlations between site occupation and hopping is investigated in a longer version of this model. The extended Hatano-Nelson model exhibits a skin effect that is weakened by correlations, which can be either increased or decreased by varying the site occupation parameter. The behavior of the model is characterized by a crossover from a short-distance skin effect to a long-distance diffusive behavior. The impact of correlations on the skin effect is found to be highly dependent on the site occupation parameter.

This study examines how listeners perceive the competence of synthesized female speech when it is created from varying combinations of two distinct voices. We found that listeners rate synthesized speech as more competent when it is produced by a combination of voices that is closer to a standard reference voice. Furthermore, we discovered that listeners are more likely to perceive synthesized speech as competent when it is created from a combination of voices that is more similar to the standard reference voice in terms of its prosodic patterns.

A novel model of dark matter is presented, where a complex scalar field interacts with a standard model field through a mediator, and is also coupled to a non-relativistic fermion. The stability of dark matter arises from a discrete symmetry, and the model's parameters are constrained by requirements of stability and the correct relic density. The model's properties are further explored, and its prospects for detection at colliders and in direct detection experiments are examined.

This research investigates the impact of the minimal length parameter on the energy levels of triaxial nuclei, specifically within the framework of the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov (HFB) mean-field theory. By incorporating the minimal length parameter into the HFB Hamiltonian, we derive the energy levels of the nuclei, which exhibit a dependence on the angular momentum. Our findings indicate that the energy levels of the nuclei are influenced by the shape of the nuclei and the value of the minimal length parameter.

This research paper presents a comprehensive method for constructing a pair of quaternary Golay complementary array (GCA) pairs within a specific, finite field-based framework. We establish the feasibility criteria for such pairs and provide a detailed, step-by-step construction process. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of our method by creating pairs of GCAs of lengths 2^k + 2^j + 2^i + 2^l for various values of k, l, j, and i, specifically for lengths 32, 48, 56, 64, 72, 80, 88, 96, and 112.

This study compares the performance of unsupervised change detection methods to their supervised counterparts, with a focus on the implications of using large amounts of unlabeled data. We examine the potential benefits of using unsupervised methods, which can operate without manual labels, in scenarios where data is abundant but annotating it is time-consuming and costly. We also investigate the limitations of these methods, which often rely on simplifying assumptions that can lead to suboptimal results. We demonstrate that, under certain conditions, unsupervised change detection can be as effective as supervised methods, but only when the data is well-suited to the approach. We also show that, in certain cases, unsupervised change detection can be less effective than supervised methods, particularly when the data does not meet the required conditions.

A new approach to scaling viscosity in non-associating molecular fluids is developed, 
grounded in the principle of density scaling for viscoelastic properties. This method
is applied to a range of non-associating molecular fluids, revealing that density
scaling yields accurate results for viscosity across various states of matter, 
including liquid, supercritical, and subcritical states. This approach is found to
be consistent with experimental data for non-associating molecular fluids, 
demonstrating its potential as a reliable and efficient method for viscosity 
modelling.

In the periodic cosmology model, the properties of the universe change according to a predetermined pattern, with the Lambda-CDM model describing the universe's early behavior up to a specific time, after which it transitions into a de Sitter phase, and then eventually shifts to a different state characterized by a positive cosmological constant. This model's behavior is studied in detail, with a focus on the transition from one phase to another, and the analysis reveals that the universe undergoes a complex series of changes, including a period of inflation, a shift to a state with a negative cosmological constant, and a subsequent transition into a Lambda-CDM model, with the possibility of a universe with a positive cosmological constant that is eventually replaced by a de Sitter phase.

The debate over nonlocality in quantum mechanics has been ongoing, with some arguing that nonlocality is inherent to quantum theory and others suggesting that it can be avoided through alternative interpretations. This paper aims to clarify the relationship between nonlocality, counterfactual measurements, and measurement independence by examining the principles of quantum mechanics and their implications for local realism.

The widespread adoption of smart speakers and wearable devices has created a need for neural networks that can run efficiently on devices with limited resources. However, the large size of these models, coupled with their high computational and memory demands, poses significant challenges. This paper explores the feasibility of implementing neural networks on devices like smart speakers and wearables, with a focus on the trade-offs between model accuracy and resource requirements. We examine the impact of model compression and pruning on the performance of these networks, and discuss the potential for future advancements.

This study presents a cluster expansion for the dimer model on isoradial graphs, utilizing a novel cluster structure that incorporates the graph's face geometry. The expansion's term-by-term matching with the prior cluster expansion of Kenyon and Wilson yields a new proof of the model's convergence towards the Kramers-Wannier topological order. The analysis also reveals a new understanding of the model's convergence rate, which is determined by the graph's minimum face angle.

The Group Lasso algorithm is a popular method for selecting variables in the context of grouped data.  In this paper, a new approach is developed to extend the Group Lasso for continuous and categorical data.  A novel algorithm is proposed to solve the Lasso problem, and its convergence properties are rigorously established.  The method is further enhanced by incorporating an iterative hard thresholding technique, which is shown to be efficient and effective.  The performance of the method is evaluated through simulations and real-world applications, including a study on the effects of air pollution on respiratory health and a categorical data analysis on the relationship between smoking and cancer.

T-Visor is a hypervisor designed for embedded systems, which can efficiently manage multiple real-time tasks with diverse scheduling needs. It achieves this by utilizing a scheduling framework that dynamically allocates time slots based on task priorities. This framework is flexible and can be easily adapted to various scheduling algorithms, such as Rate Monotonic and Earliest Deadline First. In this paper, we present a scheduling framework for T-Visor, which is capable of supporting multiple scheduling algorithms and efficiently managing real-time tasks with complex requirements.

Capturing a complete 360-degree view of a scene is crucial for creating seamless and high-quality panoramic images. Traditional methods often rely on a single camera, but this approach can be hindered by obstacles and the need for precise calibration. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel technique that utilizes a smartphone with an IMU and a wide-angle lens to capture and stitch images. By leveraging the IMU's data, we can accurately determine the camera's position and orientation, enabling the creation of panoramic images even when the camera is moved erratically. Our approach is demonstrated through both simulated and real-world testing, showcasing its effectiveness in producing high-quality 360-degree views.

In a network of identical oscillators, a stable chimera state is achieved when a subset of oscillators synchronize while others remain desynchronized. This study examines the effect of increased heterogeneity among oscillators on the stability of chimeras within non-fully connected networks. Our findings indicate that greater heterogeneity enhances the stability of chimeras, particularly in networks with a small number of non-fully connected links. This outcome is attributed to the increased differences in oscillator frequencies, which contribute to the stability of the desynchronizing subset.

This research focuses on the issue of developing a controller that can withstand disturbances in a system where the dynamics are not fully understood. We demonstrate that a controller initially designed using a simplified model of the system's dynamics can be vulnerable to unexpected events. We propose a new approach to resolve this problem by incorporating a requirement that the noise level in the system's model has a minimum value. This condition is crucial in ensuring that the controller remains effective even when the system's behavior deviates from the predicted model. We show that this method can be applied to a variety of systems and that it is possible to design a controller that can adapt to changing conditions. We also provide a mathematical proof that the proposed method can be used to develop a robust controller.

This paper introduces a novel approach to creating a family of algebras associated with a quiver and its mutation network, which generalizes the concept of Weyl groups and root systems. This method is inspired by the work of Prokofiev, who previously developed a theory for mutation networks rooted in type A. Our approach is based on the idea of a modified root system, which is constructed using matrix and tensor algebras, and is then applied to the study of quivers and their mutation networks. This theory is further refined through the use of a modified version of the Cartan-Killing form, which is used to establish a connection between the representation theory of the Weyl group and the modified root system.

In the context of random tensor networks, the entanglement spectrum within a specific region can be analyzed through the R'enyi entanglement spectrum. This analysis reveals that the reflected R'enyi spectrum exhibits a distinct pattern, characterized by a gradual decrease in the eigenvalues, as opposed to the typical random pattern observed in the standard R'enyi spectrum. This anomaly is attributed to the influence of the network's connectivity, which is particularly evident in the case of the 2D Ising model.

We investigate the probability of long-term survival in extensive collections of complex systems, where the parameters are randomly distributed, and the systems are subject to random perturbations. Our research reveals that, under certain conditions, the likelihood of long-term survival can be precisely quantified, even in complex systems, and that this probability is not influenced by the specific characteristics of the systems, such as their dimension or the nature of their attractors.

We have developed a comprehensive framework for understanding the structure of parameter space in quadratic diffeomorphisms, which has far-reaching implications for the study of bifurcations in one-dimensional maps. By focusing on the dynamics of periodic orbits, we have created a detailed classification system for the different regions of parameter space, which are separated by various bifurcation points. Our work has significant theoretical and practical applications, as it provides a foundation for studying the stability of these periodic orbits and their associated invariant sets.

The concept of holonomy in gauge theory has been well-established and widely applied. In contrast, its application in gravity has been less clear, with some researchers suggesting it's not relevant. However, a recent study has found that holonomy does have a role in gravity, but its interpretation differs significantly from that in gauge theory.

This paper examines the asymptotic behavior of the cumulative distribution functions of the sample correlation coefficient and the maximum of the absolute values of the sample autocorrelations for large random samples.

A novel approach to calculating the tunneling time is presented, which takes into account the relationship between tunneling and spin fluctuations. This approach is applied to a two-level quantum system, where the tunneling time is found to be influenced by the system's initial spin state. When the system is initially in a superposition of spin states, the tunneling time is found to be averaged over the different possible states. This average tunneling time is found to be consistent with the time it takes for the wave packet to pass through a barrier, as determined by the Landau-Vlasov equation.

We've developed a novel Ramsey interferometry technique utilizing nonlinear Hadamard gates to measure the phase shift in a Bose-Einstein condensate. By applying these gates, which are more resilient to noise than linear gates, we can significantly boost the measurement precision. Our research demonstrates that the application of nonlinear gates can increase the measurement precision by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$, resulting in a substantial enhancement of the signal-to-noise ratio. Furthermore, we've found that the application of nonlinear gates can increase the measurement precision by a factor of $\sqrt{3}$ when accounting for the effects of noise.

We examine the degeneracies of vacua in the context of the EBMS charges, which are based on soft news and Schwarzian modes. Our analysis reveals that these degeneracies are consistent with the predictions of the EBMS framework. We also explore the relationship between the degeneracy of vacua and the EBMS partition function, which is proportional to the degeneracy.

This study introduces an innovative ensemble method that enhances neural network classification by combining the strengths of two distinct training approaches: traditional gradient descent and an evolutionary strategy. The proposed technique, known as ES-GD, utilizes a novel hybrid training framework where a neural network is simultaneously trained using both gradient descent and an evolutionary strategy. The ES-GD approach is designed to leverage the complementary benefits of these two methods, with the evolutionary strategy driving the search for better solutions and the gradient descent efficiently refining the parameters. The ES-GD method is evaluated on a range of benchmark datasets and compared to both the evolutionary strategy and gradient descent alone. The results demonstrate that ES-GD achieves superior classification accuracy compared to the individual training methods, with significant improvements on certain datasets.

We establish a proof that in a Riemannian manifold with a metric of positive scalar curvature, generalized connections that are compatible with the metric must also be compatible with a Ricci flat metric. This outcome is analogous to a previous finding by Gao and Gover, which involved a specific metric, and we expand upon their work by removing the constraint of a fixed metric.

A polynomial function over a finite field is defined as a mapping from the field's power set to itself. A complete mapping is a polynomial function that hits every possible value in the power set at least once. Researchers have found that complete mappings exist for power sets of size $q^k$ where $k$ is 2 or greater, and they've also discovered a way to construct these mappings using a specific type of matrix called a Hadamard matrix.

Human visual inspection for intestinal parasites is often plagued by inaccuracies, 
despite being the standard diagnostic method in many developing countries. 
To address this, a new approach is presented, combining a machine learning 
technique with a human expert to improve overall diagnostic precision. 
A novel algorithm, specifically designed for use in low-resource settings, 
is introduced to automate the identification of intestinal parasites. 
This method, which relies on a single image per parasite, achieves high 
accuracy in classifying the parasites, even when dealing with limited data. 
To further enhance diagnostic accuracy, a new method is proposed for 
combining human and machine learning results. This approach, which is 
evaluated using real-world data from a low-resource setting, demonstrates 
the potential for significant improvement in diagnostic accuracy.

This study focuses on resolving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations, a type of nonlinear integro-differential equations, by employing a variational approach. We introduce a new method of dynamic programming that utilizes a specific type of function, called a viscosity solution, to tackle these equations. This method is then applied to a control problem involving a system of two interconnected vehicles, with the goal of minimizing the cost function subject to constraints.

This research introduces a novel quadcopter control system that incorporates a Genetic Filter to mitigate the impact of external disturbances. The control system utilizes a Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller, which is enhanced by the Genetic Filter to improve its performance. The Genetic Filter is a robust estimation technique that utilizes a Genetic Algorithm to optimize the parameters of a state observer, enabling it to accurately estimate the system's state variables in the presence of disturbances. The effectiveness of the proposed control system is demonstrated through simulations conducted in the Simulink environment, which reveal that the Genetic Filter significantly improves the quadcopter's performance, particularly in the presence of external disturbances.

The pion-nucleon sigma term, a crucial parameter in nuclear physics, has been a focus of recent research.  A new approach to determine this parameter has been developed, using lattice QCD and the Feynman-Hellmann theorem.  By analyzing the energy shift of nucleons in the presence of a finite volume and a pion mass perturbation, the sigma term can be calculated.  This method has been successfully tested in the quenched QCD and applied to the full QCD with two mass-degenerate quarks.  Furthermore, the method has been extended to the case of a finite lattice volume and a non-zero chemical potential.

The CMS detector's silicon pixel detector underwent significant upgrades 
between 2017 and 2018, which involved the installation of four new modules 
equipped with the CMS pixel detector's current technology. This upgrade 
enhanced the detector's capabilities, allowing it to handle the increased 
collision rates at the HL-LHC. This document outlines the steps taken to 
integrate the upgraded detector modules into the CMS data management system, 
including the creation of a new data format and the development of a custom 
reconstruction software. This document also discusses the CMS pixel detector's 
performance during the HL-LHC's first run, which took place in 2018.

We have developed a novel approach to classify AGN host galaxies based on their morphological characteristics. This method utilizes a deep learning technique, specifically a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), to distinguish AGN hosts from non-AGN hosts. Our approach was tested using a dataset of 1,000 AGN host galaxies and 1,000 non-AGN host galaxies, each with a size of 32x32 pixels, derived from the COSMOS field. Our results indicate that the classification precision is approximately 80% for AGN hosts at redshifts between 0.5 and 1.5, and around 70% for redshifts above 1.5. Conversely, the classification precision for non-AGN hosts is around 80% for redshifts below 1.5, and approximately 70% for redshifts above 1.5.

The effect of nuclear short-range correlations on the neutron skin thickness in neutron-rich nuclei is investigated using the high-precision Gogny-Hartree-Fock approach. The study reveals that these correlations significantly impact the neutron skin thickness, particularly in nuclei with extreme asymmetry. The research also shows that the Gogny-Hartree-Fock approach accurately captures the neutron skin thickness in certain nuclei, including those with high symmetry, and provides a reliable estimate for others, including those with low symmetry. The study's findings are compared with data from other models and experiments, and the results are discussed in relation to the properties of neutron-rich nuclei.

Our method also facilitates the efficient computation of image rotations and translations, making it suitable for applications where speed is a concern. A predictive model's ability to withstand the addition of synthetic features is a key indicator of its robustness. In this study, we examine the relationship between the stability of a model and its performance when synthetic features are introduced. Our analysis reveals that a model's stability is directly correlated with its performance when synthetic features are added. Notably, a model's performance can be maintained even after the addition of synthetic features, which are generated using various methods.

We have developed a variational quantum model that can be trained using gradient-based optimization, and we have tested its performance on a range of quantum systems. Our model, which is based on a multilayer perceptron, can be trained on complex quantum states and we have found that it can accurately predict properties such as energy and magnetization. However, we have also found that the model's performance is limited by the choice of output, with energy predictions being much more accurate than magnetization predictions. This is because energy predictions are based on a single value, whereas magnetization predictions are based on multiple values. As a result, we have found that the model's scalability is limited by the number of output values, and we have suggested that future models should focus on outputs that are more efficient to compute.

This paper focuses on identifying warped product Sasakian submanifolds within a locally conformal almost Hermitian manifold. We establish a key theorem that categorizes these submanifolds based on their semi-slant structure, and we demonstrate that only three types of warped products can exist: real, complex, and Cauchy-Riemann.

A novel approach to detecting coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus interactions is proposed, utilizing a particle detector located near a nuclear reactor. This concept leverages the significant flux of neutrinos emitted by the reactor to facilitate a high-statistics measurement of CEvNS. By employing a detector with a large volume and high purity of target material, such as liquid argon or a similar medium, this approach can achieve a high sensitivity to neutrino-nucleus interactions. This sensitivity is comparable to existing experiments, yet with a notable advantage in terms of cost-effectiveness.

Furthermore, we find that the $u=2/7$ state magnetorotons are characterized by a unique, non-zero chirality constant, which is in contrast to the $u=2/9$ state.

This research examines the dynamics of an epidemic on a network with nodes connected by edges representing various transmission risks. We establish a general framework for analyzing the model's behavior on any given network, and provide a detailed analysis of the model's long-term behavior on a specific type of network.

We examine the impact of point sources on CMB maps generated using biased estimators, which are commonly employed in CMB data analysis. Our findings indicate that strong sources can lead to significant errors in certain regions, while weak sources tend to have a more uniform impact. which outperforms both adaptive and random protocols in terms of efficiency.
The design's effectiveness is demonstrated through a comparison of its 
sensitivity to measurement errors with those of the other two methods.
The results show that the Bayesian approach surpasses the adaptive protocol 
by a factor of 2.8 and the random protocol by a factor of 3.6 in terms of

In complex networks, identifying key nodes is crucial for understanding network dynamics and structure. A new centrality measure, Gromov centrality, has been developed to capture the influence of nodes in networks by analyzing their connections to communities and subgraphs. This approach is flexible and can be applied to various network types, including those with different geometric properties. By comparing Gromov centrality to other centrality measures, researchers found that it effectively identifies key nodes in different network types, such as social and biological networks.

This theory is based on the concept of a massive, unseen object located at a great distance from the solar system, which is believed to be responsible for the observed phenomena.

This study examines the closure of bundles of matrix polynomials, focusing on the preservation of spectral properties within these closures. We demonstrate that bundles of matrix polynomials are not generally topologically closed, but we identify specific sub-classes of matrix polynomials for which the closure does preserve spectral information. We also show that bundles of matrix polynomials are not generally open under certain factorizations, but we identify a particular factorization for which the openness property holds.

In non-geometric string theory, a specific type of algebra known as continuous-trace algebras is crucial for understanding classical T-duals. This method involves a geometric process that mirrors the T-dual transformation, and we have also identified a condition under which the constructed algebra corresponds to a specific type of module algebra.

We introduce a novel method for embedding graphs with bounded treewidth into the plane in a way that preserves distances, leading to faster algorithms for problems related to Baker's work. Specifically, this allows us to improve the running times for Baker's problems in minor-free graphs, reducing the time from O(n^(1.5 log n)) to O(n log n).

This study examines the convergence of solutions to time-periodic parabolic equations with boundary conditions, focusing on the impact of initial conditions and the relative measure of the domain. We demonstrate that under certain conditions, the solutions converge to a unique periodic solution, and the convergence rate is determined by the initial conditions' proximity to the periodic solution. We also show that the convergence is influenced by the initial conditions' prevalence and the relative measure of the domain.

A quantum embedding approach, QEB-ADAPT-VQE, has been developed for efficiently solving large-scale quantum many-body problems. This method is based on the ADAPT-VQE protocol, which dynamically adjusts the quantum circuit size according to the system's energy. The original ADAPT-VQE protocol was designed for fermionic systems, but it can be inefficient due to the high cost of fermionic circuit preparation. To address this issue, a new protocol, qubit-ADAPT-VQE, was introduced, but it may not always achieve the optimal convergence speed. The QEB-ADAPT-VQE protocol is a hybrid approach that combines quantum embedding and ADAPT-VQE, allowing for the efficient preparation of fermionic circuits. This method is applied to the study of a 20-site Hubbard model, and it is found that it can achieve a significant speedup compared to the original ADAPT-VQE protocol.

Furthermore, the DGD can be easily integrated into existing supervised models to enhance their performance, as demonstrated on several benchmark datasets.

This study investigates the potential of unsupervised speech synthesis using a single speaker's voice as input, without access to paired text and audio data. A novel approach is presented, leveraging a pre-trained language model and a neural network that generates speech from text, with the goal of minimizing the gap between the input speaker's voice and the synthesized speech. A comparison with a supervised system is conducted, using both objective metrics and human evaluations of the synthesized speech. The results indicate that the unsupervised system produces speech that is nearly as intelligible and natural-sounding as the supervised system, with a notable exception in terms of speaker similarity.

The Tsallis holographic dark energy model, with its constant parameter $q$ and interacting coupling parameter $\beta$, is investigated in the context of the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker universe. A modified version of the model, with an interacting coupling parameter dependent on time, is also explored. This parameter, $\beta$, is found to be directly related to $q$ and the model's Hubble parameter, $H$. Furthermore, the model's behavior is analyzed in terms of its stability and the conditions required for its validity.

The Investment Ratio (IR) is a metric used to assess the quality of solutions to optimization problems by comparing the cost of the solution to the value it generates. IR is defined as the ratio of the solution's cost to its profit, with a lower value indicating better performance. IR is a significant indicator of a solution's quality, and it's essential to understand how it changes in response to varying problem parameters. This study focuses on analyzing the impact of parameter variations on IR by using a multidimensional approach, which involves examining how IR changes across different dimensions. This approach is demonstrated through a case study involving a real-world problem, and it's shown that the multidimensional analysis can provide valuable insights into the behavior of IR.

In the framework of synthetic differential geometry, we define a source path as a morphism with a codomain of groupoids, whose source and target maps have right inverses. A source simply connected groupoid is a source path groupoid whose source map is a covering map. A morphism of source simply connected groupoids is a morphism that preserves the source simply connected property. We establish that the category of source simply connected groupoids is equivalent to the category of simplicial groups, with the equivalence mapping to the étale groupoids.

The Dynaswap project is a blockchain-based decentralized file sharing platform, which is being developed to address the security vulnerabilities associated with cloud-based file sharing services. Dynaswap's architecture is designed to integrate multiple security features, including smart contract security, network security, and access control. To enhance security, Dynaswap incorporates advanced technologies such as multi-level encryption, digital signatures, and IPFS. Additionally, the project employs a multi-layered defense system that utilizes a gateway to filter incoming requests and a proxy server to protect the backend. Furthermore, Dynaswap's architecture includes a firewall to prevent unauthorized access and a honeypot to detect and prevent potential security threats.

Our research introduces a novel approach to sentiment analysis, combining

improve the capture of nuanced sentiment in product reviews. This method
involves pre-training a model on a large dataset of product reviews, using
contrastive learning to enhance the model's ability to distinguish between
positive and negative sentiment. The model is then fine-tuned on a smaller
dataset of reviews with sentiment labels, to improve its accuracy in
capturing subtle sentiment nuances. The results show that this approach
significantly improves the model's accuracy in capturing sentiment on a
variety of product categories, outperforming traditional methods by a
substantial margin.

The study examines the impact of reduced stomach acid production on the onset of listeriosis in immunocompromised individuals. A mathematical model is developed to simulate the dynamics of Listeria monocytogenes growth in the human stomach and blood, taking into account the bacteria's ability to evade the immune system. The model reveals that the bacteria's ability to survive inside host cells is the primary factor influencing the severity of the infection. The study also finds that the use of stomach acid suppressors can accelerate the onset of listeriosis, potentially leading to a more severe infection.

This study examines the impact of hardware impairments on secure multiuser systems utilizing intelligent reflective surfaces, which can adjust their elements to enhance secrecy. A novel approach is developed to account for these impairments in the context of a multiuser system, where a central controller allocates resources to maximize the minimum level of security for each user. A novel algorithm is proposed to solve this optimization problem, which is based on a geometric approach and is shown to be effective in improving overall security. Simulation results confirm that this approach significantly enhances the minimum level of security for each user and outperforms existing solutions.

This paper introduces a novel approach to learning, inspired by the concept of hindsight summarization, where past experiences are reinterpreted in the context of subsequent knowledge acquisition. The framework, called Hindsight Learning, aims to minimize prediction errors by leveraging the benefits of hindsight summarization. Theoretical foundations for Hindsight Learning are established, and its potential is demonstrated through the application of a simple neural network model. The model's efficacy is evaluated in the context of a basic classification task, and its performance is compared to that of a traditional learning method. The results indicate that Hindsight Learning can lead to improved performance, and its underlying mechanisms are worthy of further exploration.

The solar wind's energy source is still a topic of debate, particularly when it comes to the high-energy particles found in the solar wind. To better understand this, researchers have been studying the energy distributions of solar wind particles at various close approaches to the Sun, including at 1 AU, 0.3 AU, and 0.15 AU. By analyzing data from the Wind, Helios 2, and Helios 1 spacecraft, they found that the energy patterns at the closer distances were significantly different from those observed at 1 AU, with higher-energy particles more prevalent at the closer distances. This suggests that the solar wind's energy source is not consistent across the entire heliosphere, with the energy patterns changing as one approaches the Sun.

In a quantum-optomechanical system with a $q$-deformed optical model, the behavior of the probe field is examined as it interacts with a two-level atom and a mechanical oscillator. Additionally, the system's susceptibility is found to be highly dependent on the tunneling parameter, which can be adjusted to produce multiple peaks in the susceptibility spectrum.

This phenomenon is attributed to the differing nature of the R-negative and R-positive states, which are characterized by distinct collective and single-particle components.

By analyzing the tidal features' morphology and connection to companion galaxies, we found that 71% of the galaxies with tidal features had a clear link to a companion, while 29% did not. Furthermore, we discovered that the proportion of galaxies with tidal features increases with mass, from 25% of low-mass galaxies to 80% of high-mass galaxies. The Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG) is a novel, non-relativistic framework for understanding gravitational forces. This theory is based on a unique approach to gravitational potential, which is characterized by a specific mathematical structure. In this paper, we examine the implications of ASTG for the dynamics of massive stars, particularly in relation to the formation of these stars. One of the key challenges associated with massive star formation is the radiation problem, which is addressed by ASTG through the introduction of a new, non-standard boundary condition. This condition is analogous to the traditional boundary condition used in General Relativity, but with a key difference. By applying this boundary condition, we find that the gravitational field is characterized by a specific, non-standard behavior, which is distinct from the predictions made by General Relativity.

Simultaneous observations of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) with optical and radio frequencies can provide crucial insights into the emission mechanisms behind these events. By combining data from the CHIME/FRB, the 5 GHz, and the 2.3 GHz radio telescopes with the Zwicky Transient Facility, we conducted a comprehensive search for optical counterparts of 14 FRBs. Our research yielded no confirmed optical counterparts, but we did detect a possible optical emission from one FRB, FRB 20191127A, with a 2.5 sigma confidence level. This finding is consistent with the predictions of the "magnetar model" and the "relativistic reconnection model", but it does not support the "cannonball model". Our study also set new constraints on the emission models, including the "magnetar model" and the "cannonball model", and it established a new constraint on the "relativistic reconnection model".

The complex nature of high-power CPA and NLO-based laser systems makes it difficult to model them accurately. This is due to the intricate interplay of multiple nonlinear effects, such as Kerr lensing, self-phase modulation, and other phenomena. To address this challenge, researchers have developed a simplified approach to modeling these systems, which involves breaking down the nonlinear interactions into manageable components. This method, known as the "coupled rate equations" approach, has been successfully applied to modeling Kerr-lens mode-lockers and has been further refined to account for additional nonlinear effects. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the coupled rate equations approach, highlighting its strengths and limitations, and providing a framework for its application to various NLO-based laser systems.

We introduce the MAGIC framework, a novel approach to generating text that is both contextually relevant and visually guided. Unlike existing methods, MAGIC leverages a cross-modal attention mechanism to ensure generated text remains coherent and connected to the context. Additionally, MAGIC incorporates a visual attention module to capture the essence of an image and inform the text generation process. Through extensive testing, MAGIC consistently outperforms other text generation methods on a range of tasks, including summarization and description, even when trained on smaller datasets.

A novel approach is proposed for accurately measuring closed orbit differences between beams in a collider, leveraging direct observables that can be precisely measured. This method is particularly suited for detecting closed orbit distortions caused by non-linear effects, such as those resulting from non-linear optics, non-linear beam-beam interactions, and other sources. The approach is demonstrated through its application to the Fermilab Main Injector, with the aim of identifying and isolating the source of a significant closed orbit distortion.

In modeling the complex history-dependent plasticity of solids, researchers often employ machine learning models that require extensive training on a vast amount of data. However, these models frequently overlook the fact that real-world data is not always readily available, necessitating a more efficient approach to learning from limited data. To address this challenge, we propose a novel method for continual learning that leverages a combination of neural networks and physics-informed neural networks. This approach enables the modeling of plasticity behavior using only a small dataset, effectively capturing the intricate dependencies between material inputs and outputs. To validate the efficacy of our method, we applied it to a specific problem involving the plastic deformation of a material under varying stress conditions. Our results demonstrate that this approach can accurately model the material's behavior using a significantly reduced dataset, outperforming traditional machine learning models in the process.

The properties of the bottomonium state $\Upsilon(10753)$ are examined using the $^3\mathrm{C}_1^{[8]}$ and $^1\mathrm{D}_2^{[8]}$ potentials. These potentials are derived from the $b\bar b$ system using the basis light-front quantization method. The results indicate that the $\Upsilon(10753)$ does not fit the conventional bottomonium assignments, as it cannot be explained by the $^3\mathrm{C}_1^{[8]}$ or $^1\mathrm{D}_2^{[8]}$ states.

Training quantized neural networks with a fixed bit budget is a common practice
for reducing model size and computational costs. However, the conventional
training methods for such networks are inefficient and prone to overfitting. In
this study, we introduce a novel training method called AskewSGD, which addresses
these issues by incorporating a dynamic quantization scheme that adapts to
each layer's requirements. Our approach, AskewSGD, significantly outperforms
existing methods in terms of both accuracy and model size, as demonstrated on
various image classification tasks.

The development of robots that can adapt and change shape, like the bodies of certain animals, has been a focus of research in the field of robotics. This paper explores the potential of robots made from soft materials that can be controlled by fluid pressure, similar to the bodies of certain invertebrate and vertebrate animals. By comparing the shapes of these animals to robots that have been designed, the study highlights the need for more research into the design of these robots. This could involve using computer simulations to design robots that are more effective, or studying the shapes of these animals to gain a better understanding of their capabilities.

The Jacobi group's left-invariant metrics are directly linked to the Kähler balanced metrics on the Siegel-Jacobi upper half-space. This connection is established through a group homomorphism from the Jacobi group to the symplectic group, which preserves the metric. This relationship enables the transfer of metrics from the Siegel-Jacobi upper half-space to the Jacobi group, resulting in a specific metric that is invariant under the Siegel congruence subgroup.

To enhance the effectiveness of fact verification, we propose a novel approach that simplifies complex statements by breaking them down into more manageable components. This technique is inspired by the way humans naturally interpret and understand statements. By applying this method, we can significantly reduce the complexity of statements, which in turn enables models to process them more efficiently. Experimental results on the WikiFact and SciFact datasets demonstrate that our approach yields substantial improvements, with a notable increase in F1 score of 6.4 and 4.4 points respectively.

We introduce a novel framework for pre-training generative models on unlabeled data without relying on annotated information. This approach leverages unlabeled data to learn a distribution that captures the underlying structure of the task, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on a range of tasks, including image and text generation. Our experiments reveal that this method surpasses existing techniques in both image and text generation, and we provide a theoretical explanation for its performance by showing that it learns a distribution that is relevant to the task at hand.

We examine the efficiency of three non-symmetrizable rejection-free algorithms: hit-and-run, whitened slice sampling, and slice sampling. Through a theoretical analysis, we find that hit-and-run and whitened slice sampling generally perform better than slice sampling. Additionally, we compare the computational requirements of these methods in the context of a Bayesian model selection problem and a Bayesian regression model, where we find that whitened slice sampling is the most efficient.

In a graph with vertices and edges, a fault-tolerant distance label for a vertex v is a value assigned to it, allowing it to provide an approximate distance between any two vertices, including its own, with a guaranteed maximum error of Δ. This concept was first introduced in a 2019 study, which focused on developing efficient algorithms for creating these labels on specific graph types. This study builds upon that foundation by investigating the creation of fault-tolerant distance labels on general graphs with a guaranteed maximum error of Δ. It demonstrates that such labels can be created in a time proportional to n^(1+ε) for any given ε, no matter the graph's structure. This result is significant as it shows that such labels can be created in a time proportional to n^(1+ε) for any given ε, no matter the graph's structure.

The Fourier transforms of HBT correlations in a driven Bose-Hubbard model reveal the characteristics of the dissipative phase transition, where the emergence of a condensate is marked by a sharp peak that shifts in response to changes in the system's parameters.

This study presents a new approach to solving the Dirichlet problem for linear elliptic equations in complex domains characterized by a power growth rate in coefficients and nonlinear right-hand side terms. The method relies on a combination of the Sobolev embedding theorem and a compactness principle, allowing for a detailed analysis of the problem's solvability and regularity properties in various PDE contexts, including those involving nonhomogeneous coefficients and boundary conditions.

In neuroimaging, precise identification of brain regions is crucial for diagnosing and treating neurological disorders and understanding brain development. Current methods for segmenting brain tissues in MRI scans are often limited by their reliance on simplistic models, which can lead to inaccurate results. To address this issue, we propose a new approach that combines a deep learning technique called U-Net with a statistical model called the Gaussian Process. This integrated method, known as GP-UNet, utilizes a deep learning model to generate an initial segmentation of brain tissues and then refines it using a statistical model that takes into account the spatial relationships between different brain regions. By combining these two methods, we can achieve more accurate results than traditional approaches. Experimental results show that GP-UNet significantly outperforms other methods in terms of accuracy, especially in regions where brain tissues are difficult to distinguish.

We investigate the combined effects of bath-induced dissipation and periodic driving on a one-dimensional Bose gas, which is modeled using the dissipation-induced Floquet quantum Brownian model. This model is solved analytically to examine the impact of dissipation and driving on the system's thermodynamic properties. Our results show that the interplay between dissipation and driving can lead to the formation of a Bose-Einstein condensate, even in the presence of dissipation. Additionally, we find that the system's behavior can be described by a thermodynamic potential, which is influenced by the dissipation and driving parameters.

We examine the properties of convex functions within Orlicz spaces, specifically those that belong to the $W^{1,p}$ class. Our analysis relies on the condition $\frac{1}{p} < \frac{1}{\beta} + 1$, and we also consider the scenario where $\frac{1}{p} = \frac{1}{\beta} + 1$. In this context, we establish a relationship between the exponent $\beta$ and the function's growth rate, and we also derive a condition that must be satisfied for the function to be in the $W^{1,p}$ class.

We examine the impact of photodetection on atomic clocks that utilize two-level quantum systems, focusing on the limitations imposed by photodetection accuracy and the frequency stability of the clock. Our analysis reveals that photodetection accuracy is a critical factor in determining the overall clock performance. We also investigate the optimal photodetection strategy and the influence of photodetection on the clock's frequency stability. Our results indicate that photodetection can significantly degrade the clock's frequency stability, particularly when the photodetection accuracy is low. We propose a method to mitigate this effect by adjusting the optical pumping rate in response to photodetection events. Our findings suggest that photodetection accuracy can be improved by increasing the optical pumping rate, thereby reducing the impact of photodetection on the clock's frequency stability.

A novel algorithm, Heuristic OFES (HFES), is introduced to optimize energy consumption and network reliability through the efficient selection of network paths. HFES is a lightweight, distributed approach that leverages a simple, yet effective, mathematical model to determine the optimal path. By utilizing a linear programming method, HFES identifies the most reliable path that meets a specified energy constraint. To enhance scalability, HFES employs a distributed architecture, where each node calculates the optimal path independently. To validate HFES, simulations were conducted on a real network, demonstrating its ability to reduce energy consumption and improve reliability.

This paper introduces a novel approach to decompose the gradient of pair-wise loss in contrastive learning for image retrieval. By breaking down the loss into distinct components, each corresponding to a specific image pair comparison, the method enables the use of pre-trained models without fine-tuning. The proposed technique is based on a gradient decomposition framework that leverages the Fisher information matrix to identify the optimal direction for each loss component. The results demonstrate that this approach surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art methods, achieving top results on the widely-used ImageNet and MS-COCO benchmarks.

We investigate the connection between tensor networks and erasure correction codes, 
with a focus on codes that utilize a single type of tensor. Our analysis reveals 
that such codes, when constructed from unitary tensors, are limited to capacity 
$1/2$. Furthermore, we establish that any code with this property can be 
reproduced through a process involving a single type of unitary tensor, 
demonstrating that such codes are inherently equivalent.

Magnetized radio filaments are enigmatic, thread-like structures that crisscross the sky, spanning millions of light-years. Their origin is still shrouded in mystery, despite extensive research. Two theories have emerged to explain their formation: one suggests they are created by the interaction of magnetic fields and gas, while another proposes they are a result of the interaction between gas and magnetic fields. To shed light on this, we conducted a simulation to study how magnetic fields and gas interact, and found that the resulting patterns match those of radio filaments. Our findings indicate that the interaction between gas and magnetic fields is a viable explanation for the formation of these structures.

A novel leader-follower control strategy is proposed for a network of distributed energy resources (DERs) that are connected to a smart inverter-based grid. The approach involves a central entity, the grid operator, issuing control signals to local energy managers, who then adjust their respective DERs to meet the operator's demands. The operator's objective is to minimize the cost of energy production, while adhering to constraints on frequency stability, voltage levels, and power flow. The proposed control method is evaluated using a case study of a small inverter-based grid with 10 DERs, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in optimizing the operator's costs.

This paper presents new regret bounds for the contextual bandit problem under the assumption of a finite action space. The regret bounds are expressed in terms of the losses and delays of the best arm and are applicable to both stochastic and adversarial settings. The results are particularly useful for situations where the losses of suboptimal actions are large and the delays of the best action are minimal. The paper also provides a specific example where the regret grows at a rate of O(√(T)) in the case of stochastic losses and O(log(T)) in the case of adversarial losses.

A new theoretical framework for text generation in dialogue is proposed, which views the process as a collaborative task between the human and the machine. This framework is based on the idea that the machine acts as a facilitator, guiding the conversation towards a topic of mutual interest. To achieve this, a novel approach called Facilitated Dialogue Generation (FDG) is introduced, which involves the machine taking on a facilitator role. This is done by having the machine propose and manage a set of topics, and then generating text based on the relationship between these topics and the conversation history. Experiments with FDG on two popular dialogue datasets show promising results, and highlight the potential of this framework for improving text generation in dialogue.

Quantum chromodynamics, the theory of strong interactions, has been a cornerstone of modern physics since its inception in the 1970s. Despite significant advancements, the study of strong-interaction matter remains an uncharted territory. To address this, researchers have been exploring the properties of matter under extreme conditions, such as high temperatures and densities, using cutting-edge experimental facilities. This review will focus on the current state of knowledge regarding the phase transitions in hot and dense matter, with a particular emphasis on the role of quantum fluctuations and the potential for novel phases of matter.

The devastating impact of disasters on communities is well-documented, with a significant consequence being the loss of life and property. A disaster-stricken area requires substantial support from the public and government to aid in its recovery. A crucial factor in this recovery process is the public's perception of the effectiveness of the relief efforts. A disaster's aftermath is a critical period for the public to express their sentiments, which can be utilized to identify areas requiring more assistance. This research focuses on analyzing social media posts to gauge public sentiment towards disaster relief organizations. A dataset of 1,500 social media posts from Twitter was compiled, annotated with positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, and used to train a machine learning model. The model achieved an 80% accuracy in predicting sentiment, which can be applied to analyze large volumes of social media data in real-time. This research demonstrates the potential of combining machine learning and data-driven approaches to analyze social media sentiment, which can be applied to various domains, including disaster relief.

The R$\ell$-nilpotency degree of a group $G$ is defined as the smallest integer $n$ such that $G$ has a normal subgroup $N$ with a $\ell$-nilpotent quotient group $G/N$. This concept is further explored in the context of finite solvable groups.

A novel inversion technique has been developed to analyze the results of ultrafast experiments, which can now accurately handle noisy data and complex systems. This approach, based on a simplified model, enables the reconstruction of a system's time-dependent properties from experimental data, even when the system's behavior is difficult to predict. The method has been tested using data from a simulated experiment and has also been applied to real-world data from a study on the photoinduced phase transition in a material called VO2.

This paper presents a novel approach to driving scenario analysis by integrating a vehicle tracking system with a scenario graph. A probabilistic data association tracker is employed to identify and link vehicles within the scene, enabling the estimation of their positions and movement patterns. A scenario graph is constructed to represent the relationships between vehicles, and a Bayesian inference method is used to update the scenario state based on new data. This approach is demonstrated through a case study of a vehicle attempting to merge onto a highway.

We investigate the reflected entropy in interface conformal field theory, focusing on the entanglement between two regions separated by a boundary. Our analysis reveals that the reflected entropy exhibits universal behavior in certain situations, including when the boundary is located at a specific point and when the entanglement spans across the entire boundary. This phenomenon is analogous to the "Markov gap" observed in holographic entanglement entropy, where the rate of growth changes at a particular point. Our findings are consistent with the holographic duality and the Ryu-Takayanagi proposal, where the entanglement entropy is determined by the area of a specific geometric structure.

In systems with limited cyclic prefix and hardware imperfections, a novel channel estimation method is proposed, utilizing an improved extreme learning machine (ELM) to enhance performance. The enhanced ELM (E-ELM) method incorporates a novel kernel function and a weighted least squares (WLS) approach to achieve superior results. Theoretical analysis confirms that E-ELM has a faster convergence rate than traditional ELM, and simulations demonstrate its superior performance in various scenarios.

We examine the relationship between non-projective measurements and their equivalence to projective measurements in the context of quantum mechanics. Our approach involves deriving a set of non-projective measurements that yield results comparable to those obtained from projective measurements in specific scenarios, such as when the system is in a particular state or when the system is in a mixed state with a particular density matrix.

We demonstrate that rigid abelian G2-instantons are equivalent to those found on the cone over a del Pezzo surface, and we establish a converse to this by proving that non-abelian G2-instantons on the cone over a del Pezzo are always non-rigid.

The COVID-19 pandemic has prompted governments to implement contact tracing technologies to track the spread of the virus. These technologies, however, raise concerns about the potential for mass surveillance and the erosion of privacy. To address this issue, researchers have developed a privacy-preserving contact tracing system that utilizes blockchain technology to safeguard user data. This system allows users to create a temporary pseudonym, which is linked to a blockchain, to record interactions with others. The blockchain's decentralized nature ensures that no single entity can access user data, thereby preventing governments from exploiting the system for surveillance purposes.

The interaction between two quantum systems can be understood as a process of entangling and then de-entangling, which is influenced by decoherence. This interaction can be viewed as a form of quantum teleportation, where one system transmits information to the other through a quantum channel. This channel is essentially a quantum entanglement bridge that facilitates the transfer of quantum states. This concept is analogous to the idea of a wormhole in general relativity, where a black hole's event horizon acts as a cosmic portal, allowing for the transmission of information. This analogy is explored in the context of the black hole information paradox, with a focus on the role of wormholes as quantum communication channels.

This research paper presents a verification technique that leverages high-level language constructs to verify program correctness across different languages. The proposed method involves translating source code from one language to another, with the goal of facilitating verification. The paper demonstrates this approach using a Java program that invokes a native method written in C, with both languages utilizing the same high-level specification. The paper showcases the effectiveness of this technique by successfully verifying the Java program's correctness.

We establish an analytical continuation for the integral kernel associated with Ramanujan's identity in terms of the Hurwitz zeta function.

We establish a $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory for the action of $T$ on an elliptic curve, where $T$ is a torus. This theory is constructed as a direct product of theories for the action of $T$ on itself and the Weyl chamber, where each component is a refined version of equivariant elliptic cohomology.

In the realm of computer graphics, geometric data structures are fundamental, yet they pose a significant challenge for machine learning algorithms due to their inherent topological complexity. To address this, we propose a novel unsupervised learning approach that leverages the principles of graph theory to understand and represent these structures. By combining geometric and topological features, our method enables the creation of a unified representation that captures both the spatial and structural properties of the input data. This representation can then be utilized for downstream tasks, such as data reconstruction and completion. Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in accurately capturing the geometric and topological features of various input data, including meshes, point clouds, and simplicial complexes.

The J/psi hadroproduction cross sections at the LHC, including both direct and feed-down channels, are calculated using a factorization approach. This method involves breaking down the cross sections into two components: a short-distance coefficient and a long-distance matrix element. The short-distance coefficient is calculated using perturbative QCD, while the long-distance matrix element is determined from experimental data. By comparing the calculated cross sections with LHC data, the value of the chi_cJ and eta_c J/psi long-distance matrix elements is constrained. The results show that the eta_c J/psi long-distance matrix element is approximately 30% larger than the chi_cJ J/psi counterpart.

However, our study found that users are not aware of the purpose of this PIN and do not consider it a security measure. As a result, users do not take the PIN seriously and do not make an effort to keep it secure. In fact, many users store the PIN in an easily accessible location, such as on their phone's lock screen. Furthermore, our research discovered that users do not take the PIN as a genuine security measure and do not make any effort to protect it. In fact, users do not even bother to change the PIN when they upgrade to a new device.
